before.exam_tip_html: In Paper 2 Question 5, the examiner is looking for “conscious crafting of linguistic devices” at the top levels. This means you should deliberately plan which rhetorical appeals you will use in each paragraph before you start writing. A useful planning strategy is to annotate your plan with “E” (ethos), “L” (logos), and “P” (pathos) next to each point, ensuring you use a balanced mix across your response. Remember: the command word in Question 5 will always require you to argue a point of view, so rhetoric is not optional — it is the core skill being tested.

In Question 5, examiners are looking for deliberate crafting — not a checklist of techniques. Do not try to cram every device you know into your response. Instead, choose three or four devices that suit your audience and form, and use them with purpose. A well-placed rhetorical question followed by a powerful tricolon will impress far more than ten devices used clumsily. Remember: the mark scheme rewards “sustained crafting of linguistic devices” at Level 4. The word “sustained” means consistent quality throughout, not one brilliant sentence surrounded by flat writing. Plan which devices you will use in your introduction, body paragraphs, and conclusion before you start writing.

In Question 2, you have roughly 10 minutes. Do not waste time writing a long introduction or conclusion. Go straight into your first point. Remember: the examiner is looking for the quality of your inferences, not the quantity. Two or three well-developed paragraphs that deal with both texts and address the question’s focus will outscore five paragraphs of paraphrase. Always check: have I addressed both texts? Have I stayed on the question’s focus? Have I gone beyond what the text literally says? If the answer to all three is yes, you are on track for Level 3 or above.

In Paper 1, Section B, examiners are looking for “sustained crafting of linguistic devices” to reach Level 4. A common mistake is to use sensory language in the opening paragraph and then forget about it. Make a conscious effort to weave sensory detail, powerful verbs and “show don’t tell” throughout your entire response — not just at the start. Before you begin writing, quickly note down one detail for each sense (sight, sound, smell, taste, touch) related to your scenario. This takes 30 seconds and transforms the quality of your writing. Also, avoid naming emotions directly. Every time you catch yourself writing “I felt scared” or “she was angry,” stop and replace it with a physical reaction or sensory detail that shows the emotion instead.

In Paper 1 Question 5, examiners reward quality over quantity when it comes to figurative language. The Level 4 descriptor says “extensive and ambitious vocabulary with sustained crafting of linguistic devices.” The word “crafting” is key — it means your similes and metaphors should feel deliberate and purposeful, not thrown in randomly. Aim for two or three strong figurative moments across your whole response. Before writing a simile, ask yourself: does this create an image, match the mood, AND reveal something about the narrator or character? If it does all three, keep it. If it only does one, rethink it. And never, ever use a cliché — it signals to the examiner that you are writing on autopilot.

In Question 3, examiners want to see you analyse rather than identify. The command word is “How does the writer use language…” — this means you must explain the effect of every technique you mention. Use the What–How–Why structure: name the technique, explore its connotations, and explain the effect on the reader. Aim for 3–4 well-developed paragraphs rather than many short ones. Always stay within the given line numbers, and never retell the story. If you can explore layers of meaning in a single word — for example, unpacking both the literal and metaphorical meaning of “cannonaded” — you are operating at Level 4.

In the Paper 1 creative writing question, spend 5 minutes planning your structure before you write a single sentence. Jot down which structural moves you will use in each paragraph (D, S, Z, L). Examiners can tell the difference between writing that was planned and writing that was made up as it went along. A clear, purposeful structure is the fastest way to move from Level 2 into Level 3 or Level 4 on AO5. Remember: the mark scheme rewards “varied and inventive use of structural features” at the top level — so use at least two or three of the four moves in every response.

In Question 5, the examiner is looking for two separate things: your ideas and how accurately you write. Treat them as two separate challenges. When planning, focus entirely on what you want to say and how to structure it. When proofreading, focus entirely on technical accuracy — full stops, commas, spelling, homophones. Many students lose marks on AO6 not because they cannot spell, but because they rush and do not check. Remember: if you do not write in the correct form (e.g. you write a letter when asked for a speech), your content mark is capped at Level 2 (12 out of 24). Always underline the form, purpose and audience in the question before you begin.

In AQA Paper 1 Question 5, examiners reward deliberate structural choices just as much as beautiful language. If you use a countdown narrative, make the time pressure visible to the reader — mention a clock, use temporal markers (“Ten minutes,” “Five,” “One”), or show time through changing light or sound. This signals to the examiner that your structure is intentional, not accidental, which is the difference between Level 3 (“controlled pace”) and Level 4 (“subtle variation of pace”). Always plan your five stages before you write, and always leave 5 minutes to proofread for AO6 — those 16 marks for technical accuracy are the easiest to improve on the day.

Q4 is the only reading question that asks for your personal response. The command phrase “to what extent do you agree” means you must state your position. Do not sit on the fence without ever committing — use phrases like “I strongly agree” or “I partially agree” to anchor each paragraph. The examiner is looking for a critical voice, not a neutral summary. Remember: always refer back to the exact words in the statement, always stay within the specified lines, and always explain the effect of methods on the reader. Quality beats quantity — three perceptive paragraphs will outscore five simple ones every time.

In Paper 2 Section A, the most common reason students lose marks is poor time management — they spend too long on Q1 and Q2, then rush Q3 and Q4 which are worth the most marks. Stick to the timing plan: 5 minutes for Q1, 10 for Q2, 12 for Q3, and 18 for Q4. For Q3, remember the command word is “How” — this means analyse the effects of language, not describe what happens. For Q4, always use comparative connectives (“In contrast,” “Similarly,” “Whereas”) and write about methods as well as feelings. The mark scheme rewards “like-for-like” comparisons — if you discuss personification in Source A, compare it to personification (or another method) in Source B within the same paragraph.
